etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pecok, pekok, pocok, pacok, equivalent to pea (“peafowl; peacock”) +‎ cock. Compare Old Norse páfugl (“peacock”, literally “pea-fowl”), and English peahen, peachick, etc.

definitions.definition: A male peafowl, especially Pavo cristatus, notable for its brilliant iridescently ocellated tail.

quote.citation: 1769, Firishta, translated by Alexander Dow, Tales translated from the Persian of Inatulla of Delhi, volume I, Dublin: P. and W. Wilson et al., page v:
quote.text: The ſpring diſplaying her elegant taſte, the proud walk of the gold-feathered pheaſant, the light tread of the ſmall-hoofed hind, and the dancing of the ſtar-trained peacock, infuſed joy into the ſoul of the ſpectator of the aſtoniſhing works of the Creator.

definitions.definition: A peafowl (of the genus Pavo or Afropavo), either male or female.
A pompous or vainglorious person [from the 14th c.].
(entomology) Any of various Asian species of papilionid butterflies of the genus Papilio.
(intransitive) To strut about proudly or haughtily.

quote.citation: 2014 May 30, Will Butler, “The Mark of Cane”, in The New York Times Magazine‎[1]:
quote.text: A routine border-check in upstate New York had turned into a back-room interrogation, and I was worried, because the three friends I was traveling with didn’t respond to authority well. I could almost hear the wry grins cracking their faces as the officers peacocked. “Is U.S. Customs a joke to you?” one officer asked. My friend Alex said, “No law against smiling, sir.”

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To engage in peacocking, ostentatious dress or behaviour to impress women.
